requirements.verification_test: Interface security tests: unsigned or tampered messages from a partner are rejected. Encryption is verified in transit and at rest.

requirements.clause: 11.50(a)-(b) - Signature manifestations
requirements.requirement: Signed electronic records contain information associated with the signing that clearly indicates: (1) the printed name of the signer; (2) the date and time the signature was executed; and (3) the meaning of the signature (such as review, approval, responsibility or authorship). These items are subject to the same controls as electronic records and are included in any human-readable form of the record (electronic display or printout).
requirements.system_implications: Every signature is displayed and printed with: full printed name (not just the user ID), date and time including time zone (store UTC; show site-local with offset), and a meaning from a controlled list bound to the step ('Performed by', 'Verified by', 'Supervised/Checked by', 'Reviewed by QA', 'Approved for release', 'Rejected', 'Prepared', 'Checked', 'Approved'). The manifestation is stored immutably with the signature at signing time, not re-derived from the mutable user table, so later name changes do not alter historic signatures. Manifestations appear on every screen and report view of the signed data.
requirements.verification_test: Sign a step and view it on screen, in the batch report PDF and in the export -> all three elements appear. Rename the user -> historic signatures still show the original printed name. Signatures across time zones show the correct local time and offset.

requirements.clause: 11.70 - Signature/record linking
requirements.requirement: Electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records, are linked to their records so that the signatures cannot be excised, copied or otherwise transferred to falsify an electronic record by ordinary means.
requirements.system_implications: Each signature record binds the signer identity, meaning, timestamp and a cryptographic hash of the exact signed content (the record version). A later permitted correction of signed data automatically marks the signature 'superseded by change' and requires re-signing (the performer's or verifier's as applicable), with the audit trail kept. Signatures cannot be moved or copied between records, and the integrity job detects any such tampering. Hybrid wet-ink signatures on printouts are avoided. If unavoidable, the scanned signed page is indexed to the record ID and content hash and the hybrid process is covered by an SOP.
requirements.verification_test: Correct a signed value -> the signature status becomes superseded and re-sign is required. Copying a signature row to another record in the test database -> the integrity check fails. Hash verification succeeds for untouched records.

requirements.source: 21 CFR Part 11 (11.100(c)(1) as amended by the technical amendment of March 2, 2023)
requirements.clause: 11.100(a)-(c) - Electronic signatures: general requirements
requirements.requirement: (a) Each electronic signature is unique to one individual and is not reused by or reassigned to anyone else. (b) Before an organization establishes, assigns, certifies or otherwise sanctions an individual's electronic signature or any element of it, the organization verifies the individual's identity. (c) Persons using electronic signatures certify to FDA, before or at the time of use, that their electronic signatures are intended to be the legally binding equivalent of handwritten signatures. The certification is signed with a traditional handwritten signature and, after the 2023 amendment, submitted in electronic or paper form as described on FDA's 'Letters of Non-Repudiation Agreement' web page. Additional certification or testimony is provided on FDA request.
requirements.system_implications: User IDs are never reused or reassigned, even after deactivation; enforced by a permanent uniqueness registry across all sites and tenants. Account activation requires a recorded identity-verification step (who verified, method, date). A go-live checklist per legal entity records the non-repudiation letter submission (date, scope: company-wide or individual). Signature credentials are personal: no proxy signing or delegated signing on behalf of another person.
requirements.verification_test: Create a new account with the ID of a deactivated user -> blocked. Activate an account without an identity-verification record -> blocked. Configuration shows NRL status per legal entity.

requirements.clause: 11.200(a)(1)-(3), (b) - Electronic signature components and controls
requirements.requirement: Non-biometric e-signatures use at least two distinct identification components, such as an ID code and password. When an individual executes a series of signings during a single, continuous period of controlled system access, the first signing uses all components and subsequent signings use at least one component that only that individual can execute and that is designed for use only by that individual. Signings not performed during a single, continuous period of controlled access each use all components. E-signatures are used only by their genuine owners, and are administered so that attempted use by anyone other than the owner requires the collaboration of two or more individuals. Biometric e-signatures are designed so they cannot be used by anyone other than their genuine owners.
requirements.system_implications: The signing dialog re-authenticates at the moment of signing (user ID + password, or an SSO step-up with a second factor). The 'continuous period of controlled access' is defined strictly: any lock, timeout, logout or terminal switch ends it. Recommendation: require both components for all critical signatures (verification, QA review, release, MBR approval), because shop-floor terminals are shared. A verifier signs in the same dialog with their own full credentials; the performer's session can never supply the verifier's signature. No 'remember password'. Administrators cannot see passwords, and admin-set passwords force a change at first use (so misuse needs collusion). Biometric options, such as badge plus fingerprint in cleanrooms where typing is impractical, need liveness and anti-spoofing evidence.
requirements.verification_test: Sign twice in one session -> the second signing requires at least the password. After timeout or lock -> both components required. Try to record a verifier signature using the performer's session -> requires the verifier's own ID and password. An admin-reset password cannot be used to sign before it is changed.

requirements.clause: 11.300(a)-(e) - Controls for identification codes/passwords
requirements.requirement: Controls include: (a) keeping each combined ID code and password unique so no two individuals share the same combination; (b) periodically checking, recalling or revising ID code and password issuances (e.g., password aging); (c) loss-management procedures to electronically deauthorize lost, stolen, missing or compromised tokens, cards and other devices, and to issue replacements under suitable, rigorous controls; (d) transaction safeguards to prevent unauthorized use of passwords and/or ID codes, and to detect and report any attempted unauthorized use in an immediate and urgent manner to the system security unit and, as appropriate, organizational management; (e) initial and periodic testing of tokens or cards that bear or generate ID or password information, to ensure they work and have not been altered without authorization. Items (a)-(d) were confirmed verbatim; (e) is from the regulation text.
requirements.system_implications: Password policy: complexity, history, and aging or a documented risk-based equivalent (e.g., NIST SP 800-63B with compromised-password screening), with the rationale recorded. Account lockout after N failed login or signature attempts. Real-time security alerting (SIEM) on repeated failures, signature attempts on locked accounts, and anomalous access, routed to the security unit with acknowledgment tracking and escalation to management. Immediate revocation of lost badges or tokens, with replacement issued only after identity verification. Periodic badge and token functional tests.
requirements.verification_test: N failed signature attempts -> the account locks and an alert reaches the security unit within the defined minutes. A revoked badge cannot authenticate. Token test records exist.

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures - Scope and Application' (August 2003)
requirements.clause: Sections III.A-III.C (narrow interpretation of scope; enforcement discretion; predicate rules)
requirements.requirement: FDA interprets Part 11's scope narrowly. Part 11 applies to predicate-rule records kept electronically in place of paper; to records kept electronically in addition to paper and relied on for regulated activities (business practice decides); to records submitted electronically; and to e-signatures intended as handwritten equivalents. FDA exercises enforcement discretion on the validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying requirements, but predicate rules (e.g., 211.68, 211.180) still apply. Audit trails are particularly appropriate where users are expected to create, modify or delete regulated records during normal operation. FDA intends to enforce all other provisions, including access limits, operational, authority and device checks, training, accountability policies, documentation controls, open-system controls, and all e-signature requirements (11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, 11.300). Enforcement discretion also applies to legacy systems operational before August 20, 1997, under certain circumstances.
requirements.system_implications: Enforcement discretion is not a design basis. The eBMR is the primary record for regulated activity and users routinely create and modify GMP data, so implement every 11.10 control, including validation and full audit trails; the DI Q&A (2018) and 211.68 independently expect them. Document in an SOP or system specification that the electronic record is the official record, and treat printouts as copies. Avoid hybrid paper and electronic processes, or define them explicitly with linking controls (11.70).
requirements.verification_test: Documentation check: a record-type inventory stating the official record per data type. A risk assessment justifies any control not implemented (none expected for GMP batch data).

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Data Integrity and Compliance With Drug CGMP: Questions and Answers' (December 2018)
requirements.clause: Q1 definitions: data integrity (ALCOA), metadata, audit trail, static vs dynamic record, backup, computer or related systems
requirements.requirement: Data integrity means completeness, consistency and accuracy of data; complete, consistent and accurate data are attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded, original or a true copy, and accurate (ALCOA). Metadata is the contextual information needed to understand data and must be kept with it. An audit trail is a secure, computer-generated, time-stamped electronic record that allows reconstruction of events relating to the creation, modification or deletion of an electronic record, including record-level and system-level actions. Static records are fixed; dynamic records allow interaction (e.g., reprocessing). A backup is a true copy of the original record kept securely throughout the retention period, including associated metadata, in the original format or a compatible one; this is distinct from temporary disaster-recovery copies.
requirements.system_implications: The data model keeps each value with its metadata (units, precision, instrument, specification version, context step, timestamps, user). Dynamic data (trend and historian data, lyophilizer cycles, PAT spectra) is kept in native, reprocessable form with a viewer, not only as images. The backup design follows US-211-68B. The ALCOA attributes map to controls: attributable (unique users, device IDs), legible (rendering, no overwrite), contemporaneous (server timestamps, immediate commit), original (first capture preserved), accurate (validated calculations and interfaces).
requirements.verification_test: For sample records, confirm the metadata is complete and the native dynamic data can be re-rendered. Confirm the backup contains metadata and audit trails.

requirements.clause: Q on validation of CGMP workflows (each workflow is an intended use to be validated)
requirements.requirement: FDA expects each CGMP workflow on a computer system (e.g., creation of an electronic MPCR) to be validated for its intended use, citing 211.63, 211.68(b) and 211.110(a). Validating the system or platform alone is not sufficient. (Topic confirmed through secondary summaries of the guidance; the wording is paraphrased from the guidance text.)
requirements.system_implications: Validation covers configured workflows, not just the software product: every MBR template or building block, each site-specific configuration, interface and report used for GMP decisions (e.g., review-by-exception rules, release gate criteria, calculations). MBRs themselves need verification (a test or 'dry-run' execution, recipe verification) before they become Effective. This is a validated MBR lifecycle and should be built into the product as an MBR simulation or dry-run mode that produces no GMP records.
requirements.verification_test: An MBR cannot become Effective without a linked verification record from dry-run execution. Validation evidence exists for each GMP report and review-by-exception rule.

requirements.clause: Q on restricting access to CGMP computer systems; system administrator independence
requirements.requirement: Access to CGMP computer systems is restricted to authorized personnel. Firms should technically restrict the ability to alter specifications, process parameter data, and manufacturing or testing methods where possible. FDA suggests assigning the system administrator role, including rights to alter files and settings, to personnel independent from those responsible for record content. Where that is not possible, secondary review of settings and content is recommended.
requirements.system_implications: Separate administrative (IT/config) roles from GMP data roles, and let no single account hold both at a site by default. Specification limits, process parameters and MBR content can only change through the MBR/master-data change workflow, never through admin tools. Any exception (e.g., a small site where one person must hold both roles) requires documented approval and triggers mandatory secondary review of that person's configuration changes. Privileged activity is logged and reviewed periodically.
requirements.verification_test: Try to grant admin and QA/production roles to one account at the same site -> blocked, or requires exception approval. Change a specification limit through the admin console -> impossible. The privileged-activity review report is produced.

requirements.clause: Q on shared login accounts
requirements.requirement: FDA is concerned about shared login accounts because they prevent identification of a unique individual, so the system would not conform to parts 211 and 212, and audit trails cannot be relied on to show who entered or changed data when logins are shared.
requirements.system_implications: No generic, shared or role accounts for GMP actions, including shop-floor 'line' logins. Fast user switching on shared terminals (badge tap plus PIN/password) makes individual login practical. Machine or service accounts for interfaces are non-interactive, cannot sign, and are attributed to the device or interface. Kiosk-mode terminals still require individual authentication for every GMP entry.
requirements.verification_test: Scan the user directory for generic accounts -> none with GMP permissions. A service account attempting a signature -> blocked. On a shared terminal, each entry is attributed to the individual who authenticated.

requirements.clause: Q on control of blank forms
requirements.requirement: Blank forms (including worksheets, laboratory notebooks and MPCRs) should be controlled by the quality unit or another document-control method. For example, numbered sets of blank forms may be issued and reconciled when all issued forms are complete. Incomplete or erroneous forms should be kept as part of the permanent record with written justification for their replacement.
requirements.system_implications: The electronic equivalent is controlled issuance of batch record instances, logbooks and ad-hoc forms (e.g., deviation forms, rework sheets). Each instance is uniquely numbered, generated from an approved template version, and reconciled (issued vs completed vs voided). Voided instances stay with a reason and approver. Uncontrolled attachments (uploading unapproved spreadsheets or forms as records) are prohibited; attachments must come from controlled templates or be clearly marked as supporting information.
requirements.verification_test: The reconciliation report shows every issued instance accounted for. Voiding requires a reason and QA approval and the voided instance remains retrievable.

requirements.clause: Q on audit trail review: who and how often
requirements.requirement: FDA recommends that audit trails capturing changes to critical data be reviewed with each record and before final approval of the record. Other audit trails (e.g., system-level) are reviewed on a schedule based on system complexity and intended use. Audit trails are part of the associated records, so personnel responsible for record review under CGMP (e.g., 211.22(a), 211.101(c)-(d), 211.103, 211.182, 211.186(a), 211.192, 211.194(a)(8)) should review the audit trails of changes to that data as they review the rest of the record.
requirements.system_implications: The MBR designer flags critical data per step (e.g., weights, API lot, IPC results, yields, time/temperature, EM results, label data). The review workbench presents a filtered audit trail of every change to critical data after initial entry (old value, new value, who, when, reason) as a mandatory review section, and QA must acknowledge it before release. Verifiers at step level also see prior changes for the data they verify. A system-level audit trail review (logins, permission changes, configuration changes, failed signatures) runs periodically with a recorded review and outcome. Summary views must not hide individual changes, and full audit trail drill-down is always available.
requirements.verification_test: Change a critical value after initial entry -> it appears in the QA release review section and release is blocked until acknowledged. The periodic system audit-trail review record exists with reviewer and findings.

requirements.clause: Q on when electronic data become a CGMP record (save at time of performance; no temporary memory)
requirements.requirement: When generated to satisfy a CGMP requirement, all data become a CGMP record. Data must be documented or saved at the time of performance. Storing data electronically in temporary memory, in a way that allows manipulation, before creating a permanent record is not acceptable; data automatically saved only to temporary memory do not meet CGMP documentation or retention requirements. A LIMS or Electronic Batch Record (EBR) system can be designed to save automatically after each separate entry, similar to indelibly recording each entry contemporaneously on a paper batch record, combined with a procedure requiring entry at the time of performance.
requirements.system_implications: Each field entry or observation is committed durably to the server-side record (with audit trail) when the user submits it, not when the page, step or batch is saved. Offline or edge clients (for cleanrooms with poor connectivity) must write to a tamper-evident, append-only local journal with a trusted timestamp and sync to the server without allowing edits in between. Any edit after commit is a change with an audit trail and reason. No 'draft' state for GMP observations that lets values be changed silently before 'submit step'. Data from instruments is captured automatically at generation.
requirements.verification_test: Enter a value, then kill the browser or network before completing the step -> the value is persisted and visible with its timestamp. Change it afterwards -> the audit trail shows the original. Offline mode: entries survive device reboot and sync with the original timestamps, and local tampering is detected.

requirements.clause: Q on electronic copies as accurate reproductions / true copies; static printouts of dynamic records
requirements.requirement: Electronic copies can be used as true copies of paper or electronic records if they preserve the content and meaning of the original data, including associated metadata and the static or dynamic nature of the original records. A printout or static record does not preserve the dynamic nature of a dynamic electronic record, so it would fail CGMP requirements as a replacement.
requirements.system_implications: Archival and export must preserve dynamic data natively (e.g., historian time-series, lyophilizer cycle data, vision-system images, PAT spectra) together with metadata, not just PDF renderings. Paper-to-electronic scans (for any legacy or hybrid inputs) go through a verified true-copy process (verifier signature attesting completeness and legibility). The originals may only be destroyed if the copy is verified and the SOP allows it.
requirements.verification_test: Restore an archived batch and re-render its trend data interactively. A scanned-document workflow requires a true-copy verification signature.

requirements.clause: Q on electronic signatures in place of handwritten signatures for MPCRs
requirements.requirement: Electronic signatures with appropriate controls can be used instead of handwritten signatures or initials in any CGMP-required record. When a regulation such as 211.186(a) specifies 'full signature, handwritten', an electronic signature with appropriate controls that securely link it to the record satisfies the requirement (Part 11).
requirements.system_implications: The system may be fully paperless for MPCR preparation, checking and approval, BPR execution and release, provided the Part 11 signature controls (US-11-50, US-11-70, US-11-100, US-11-200, US-11-300) are implemented. Initials fields (e.g., 211.182 'sign or initial') are satisfied by the same e-signature mechanism.
requirements.verification_test: MBR approval and batch release are completed end to end with e-signatures, and all signature controls pass their tests.

requirements.clause: Q on invalidation/exclusion of CGMP data from decision making
requirements.requirement: CGMP data may only be excluded from decision making with a valid, documented, scientific justification. All data, including excluded or invalidated data, must be retained and available for QU review; data cannot be deleted or selectively reported.
requirements.system_implications: Invalidating an entry or IPC measurement (e.g., a mis-weighed tablet or instrument error) never deletes it. The data point is marked invalid with a mandatory scientific justification, user and timestamp, is visible in the record and the review-by-exception list, and requires QA concurrence where the SOP says so. Statistics show both included and excluded counts. Repeated-measurement ('test into compliance') patterns are flagged, e.g., multiple repeats of an IPC until it passes.
requirements.verification_test: Invalidate a value -> it stays visible and marked with the justification, and appears in the QA review list. Three repeats of the same IPC -> an automatic flag.

requirements.source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018); FDA Guidance 'Conducting Remote Regulatory Assessments - Questions and Answers' (final, June 2025)
requirements.clause: DI Q&A Q on FDA investigator access to electronic records; RRA guidance (FD&C Act 704(a)(4) records requests)
requirements.requirement: FDA investigators may review all CGMP records, including electronic records, metadata and audit trails, during inspections. FDA may request records in advance of or instead of inspections (704(a)(4)) and conduct remote regulatory assessments. The final RRA Q&A (June 26, 2025) replaced the January 2024 revised draft. (The investigator-access point is from knowledge of the DI Q&A; the RRA status is confirmed.)
requirements.system_implications: Provide a read-only 'inspector view' role (time-limited, audited) with full access to batch records, audit trails and metadata. Provide rapid, complete export packages (US-11-10B) and secure transfer for 704(a)(4) requests. Log what was provided to FDA and when.
requirements.verification_test: Create an inspector account -> it can view but not change anything and is auto-disabled at expiry. A records-request package for five batches is generated within the SLA and includes audit trails.

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Computer Software Assurance for Production and Quality (Management) System Software' - final Sept 24, 2025; revised final Feb 3, 2026 (aligned to QMSR)
requirements.clause: Risk-based assurance framework: intended use; process-risk determination (high vs not high); assurance activities (scripted, unscripted: ad hoc, error-guessing, exploratory; vendor evidence; monitoring); assurance record
requirements.requirement: FDA recommends a risk-based approach to establish confidence that automation used in production or the quality system performs as intended. Identify intended use; determine whether a feature is high process risk (failure could compromise product quality/safety) or not; choose proportionate assurance activities (scripted testing for high-risk features; unscripted or exploratory testing, leveraging vendor activities, etc., for lower risk); and keep a record of intended use, risk determination, assurance activities, issues and their disposition, conclusion, date and responsible person. The guidance was issued by CDRH and CBER for medical device production/quality system software. It supersedes Section 6 of 'General Principles of Software Validation'. The Feb 2026 revision aligns it with the QMSR (effective Feb 2, 2026) and reportedly adds explicit consideration of revalidation when software is updated (from a secondary source).
requirements.system_implications: For a drug eBMR, CSA is not binding under 21 CFR 211 (it is a CDRH/CBER device guidance), but it is a recognized risk-based model FDA endorses and can support the 211.68 and 11.10(a) validation approach. Classify eBMR features by process risk. High-risk features (scripted testing plus independent review): material status hard stops; weighing and dispense calculations (potency adjustment); dual-verification enforcement; yield and reconciliation calculations and limits; label and variable-data verification; release gate; e-signature controls; audit trail; timers; interfaces that carry GMP data; data integrity and hashing; retention and purge prevention. Not-high-risk features (unscripted/exploratory, with objective evidence): UI layout, non-GMP dashboards, help text. Automate regression suites for multi-site configurations and for every vendor release. Keep the CSA-style assurance record per release.
requirements.verification_test: The validation plan contains a risk classification of all URS items. Each high-risk item has scripted test evidence. Each vendor release has a documented assurance record (intended use, risk, activities, issues, conclusion, date, name).

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing - CGMP' (September 2004)
requirements.clause: Time limits for aseptic processing phases (Section on time limitations/validation)
requirements.requirement: Time limits should be established for each phase of aseptic processing. These include the period between the start of bulk product compounding and its sterilization, filtration processes, product exposure on the processing line, and storage of sterilized equipment, containers and closures. Total filtration time should be limited to an established maximum to prevent microorganisms from penetrating the filter. Time limits should be supported by data, and bioburden and endotoxin load should be assessed when setting them (e.g., for the formulation stage).
requirements.system_implications: The injectables MBR must require timers for at least: compounding start -> sterilizing filtration start; total filtration duration; sterilized equipment/components/closures expiry (from end of sterilization to use); product exposure on the line (e.g., fill start -> end, open-vial exposure); and stoppered -> capped. Timer limits reference validation study IDs. A breach auto-creates a deviation (US-211-111) and blocks release until dispositioned.
requirements.verification_test: An injectables MBR without the mandatory timer set -> approval blocked. Exceed the filtration time limit -> deviation created and batch flagged.

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing' (Sept 2004)
requirements.clause: Section IX.A - Process simulations (media fills): frequency, interventions, acceptance criteria
requirements.requirement: Aseptic processes are validated by process simulations. The guidance sets initial qualification with multiple (three) successful runs and semi-annual requalification per line and shift. Simulations should include activities and interventions representative of each shift and shift changeover. Acceptance: when filling fewer than 5,000 units, no contaminated units should be detected, and one contaminated unit is cause for revalidation after investigation. For 5,000-10,000 units, one contaminated unit should result in an investigation including consideration of a repeat media fill, and two are cause for revalidation after investigation. For more than 10,000 units, one contaminated unit should result in an investigation, and two are cause for revalidation after investigation.
requirements.system_implications: Support an 'Aseptic Process Simulation' batch type in the injectables edition with its own MBR: media and its growth promotion, units filled, incubation, inspection, contaminated-unit identification. Record every intervention performed, with type, time, operator and count. Keep a line/operator APS qualification status driven by results (US-211-113). Interventions during commercial batches are recorded in the BPR with type, time and personnel, so they can be checked against those qualified in the APS; an intervention type not qualified in the APS is flagged as a deviation.
requirements.verification_test: A failed APS (e.g., 2 positives in 12,000 units) -> the line status becomes Not Qualified and commercial filling is blocked. A commercial batch intervention type not in the APS-qualified list -> deviation.

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing' (Sept 2004)
requirements.clause: Section IV / Table 1 (air classifications) and Section X.A (environmental monitoring program: alert/action levels, trending, investigations)
requirements.requirement: The critical zone should meet ISO 5 (3,520 particles >= 0.5 micron per cubic meter, in operation). The area adjacent to the aseptic line should be at least ISO 7, with ISO 8 for less critical activities. Table 1 gives microbiological action levels. From recollection of the guidance, not re-verified: ISO 5 active air 1 cfu/m3 and settling plates (90 mm, 4 h) 1 cfu; ISO 6 7 and 3; ISO 7 10 and 5; ISO 8 100 and 50. The EM program should include alert/action levels, trending, investigation of excursions, and evaluation of their impact on batches.
requirements.system_implications: An EM data model links each sample (location, grade, type, time, operator for personnel samples) to the batch and time window. Limits are configured per grade from site SOPs, which may be stricter (e.g., EU Annex 1 'no growth' in Grade A). An action-level excursion in Grade A/ISO 5 during the batch window auto-creates an event requiring an investigation and batch impact assessment before release. Continuous particle monitoring alarms in the batch window are attached to the batch.
requirements.verification_test: Enter an ISO 5 viable result above the action level for a location and time inside the batch window -> an event is created and release is blocked until assessed. Adverse trends generate alerts.

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing' (Sept 2004)
requirements.clause: Section XII - Batch Record Review: Process Control Documentation
requirements.requirement: The guidance has a dedicated section on batch record review for aseptic processing (confirmed section title). From recollection of the text, not re-verified because the document could not be fetched: before batch release, the QCU review should cover all in-process and laboratory control results together with process-control documentation for the aseptic operation. That documentation includes environmental and personnel monitoring data, interventions and deviations during filling, sterilization and depyrogenation records for equipment, containers and closures, filter integrity results, and adherence to time limits. Discrepancies and excursions should be investigated and their impact on the batch assessed.
requirements.system_implications: The injectables release gate (US-211-160-167) includes an 'Aseptic process control review' checklist that is generated automatically from linked data: EM and personnel monitoring results complete and within limits or investigated; interventions reviewed; all sterilization/depyrogenation cycles for items used passed; filter integrity passed; all timers within limits; APS status valid on the fill date; particle monitoring alarms reviewed. QA must acknowledge each section.
requirements.verification_test: A batch with one pending EM result -> the aseptic review section is incomplete and release is blocked. All sections complete -> QA can proceed.

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing' (Sept 2004)
requirements.clause: Sections on filtration efficacy and sterilization of equipment, containers and closures (integrity testing; qualification/validation of cycles)
requirements.requirement: From recollection of the guidance, not re-verified: sterilizing-grade filter integrity testing can be done before processing and should be done routinely after use to detect filter leaks or perforations during processing. Sterilization and depyrogenation cycles for equipment, containers and closures should be validated and each run's physical parameters recorded and reviewed.
requirements.system_implications: Integrity tester integration captures test type (bubble point, diffusion/forward flow, pressure hold), limits, result, filter lot and instrument ID. Post-use integrity is mandatory in the MBR for sterilizing filters. Sterilizer/tunnel cycle data (time, temperature, pressure, F0, load pattern ID, validated recipe version) is linked to each load and the items it released. A failed or missing record blocks item use or batch release.
requirements.verification_test: Missing post-use integrity result -> release blocked. Cycle data outside validated parameters -> the load's items are blocked.

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Submission of Documentation in Applications for Parametric Release of Human and Veterinary Drug Products Terminally Sterilized by Moist Heat Processes' (Feb 2010); CPG Sec. 490.200
requirements.clause: Parametric release data and monitoring positions; 211.167(a) sterility testing otherwise required
requirements.requirement: FDA has accepted parametric release for moist-heat terminally sterilized products since 1985, where approved in the application. Positions in the load should be identified so the load's exposure to the sterilization process is measured and recorded against defined criteria for parametric release, with the location and number of monitors described and justified in the application. A Class 5 chemical indicator is recommended for most applications. Without an approved parametric release, 211.167(a) requires sterility testing of each batch.
requirements.system_implications: The product master has a 'release mode' attribute: sterility test or approved parametric release (with the application reference). In parametric mode, the release gate requires: the validated cycle and load pattern used; all critical parameters (time at temperature, temperature, pressure, F0 at each specified monitoring position) within limits from the sterilizer's raw data; chemical indicator results; and pre-sterilization bioburden where required. Any failed parameter means the batch cannot be released parametrically, and sterility-test release is not an allowed substitute unless the application permits it. Terminal sterilization loads are linked to the units, trays and positions they contain.
requirements.verification_test: One probe below the F0 minimum -> the parametric release criterion fails and release is blocked. A product without approved parametric release -> the gate requires a sterility result.

requirements.source: FDA 'Guide to Inspections of Lyophilization of Parenterals' (July 1993); 21 CFR 211.137(c)
requirements.clause: Lyophilization cycle and controls; cycle validation; lyophilizer sterilization
requirements.requirement: The FDA investigator guide covers the lyophilization cycle and its controls, cycle validation, and lyophilizer sterilization and design. Records of cycle data are reviewed against the validated/filed cycle (details are from recollection; the guide is a 1993 inspection reference, not a guidance). For reconstituted products, labeling bears both reconstituted and unreconstituted expiration information (211.137(c)).
requirements.system_implications: Integrate the lyophilizer SCADA/historian: recipe ID and version, and per-phase setpoints and actuals (shelf temperature, chamber pressure, condenser temperature, product thermocouple/wireless probe temperatures, pressure-rise or comparative pressure tests, phase durations). Record loading pattern and time, stoppering, and chamber sterilization/leak-test status before loading. Excursions against validated ranges auto-create deviations. Loading/unloading times feed time-limit timers. Store native cycle data as dynamic records (US-DI-08).
requirements.verification_test: Replay a cycle file with a shelf-temperature excursion -> deviation created. A chamber with no valid SIP/leak test -> loading blocked.

requirements.source: FDA draft guidance 'Inspection of Injectable Products for Visible Particulates' (Dec 2021; still draft as of 2026 per search)
requirements.clause: 100% visual inspection plus AQL sampling; lifecycle inspection program
requirements.requirement: FDA's draft recommends a holistic program in which every unit of an injectable is inspected (100% inspection, manual, semi-automated or automated), followed by statistical sampling (AQL) of accepted units to verify batch quality. Meeting a USP compendial standard alone is generally not sufficient for CGMP. USP <790> frames the 'essentially free' expectation with a sampling plan (AQL 0.65 cited in secondary sources). Defects should be classified, trended and investigated.
requirements.system_implications: The inspection step in the BPR records: units presented, units accepted, and rejects by defect category (critical, major, minor; particle type such as fiber, glass or metal; container/closure defects), inspector IDs and qualification status (manual inspection), and machine recipe and challenge-set results (automated). It then records the AQL sample size, acceptance and rejection numbers, and results. The system calculates the reject rate against alert/action limits. AQL failure -> reinspection only if allowed by SOP, with a deviation, and reinspection counts are recorded separately. Units accounted for: filled = accepted + rejected + samples + destroyed, within limits.
requirements.verification_test: Enter reject counts above the action limit -> deviation. AQL result exceeding the acceptance number -> batch hold. The unit accountability equation must balance.

requirements.source: FDA Guidance 'Process Validation: General Principles and Practices' (January 2011, Revision 1)
requirements.clause: Stage 2 (PPQ) and Stage 3 (Continued Process Verification) - data collection and trending
requirements.requirement: Stage 3 provides ongoing assurance in routine production that the process stays in a state of control. FDA recommends continued monitoring and sampling of process parameters and quality attributes at the level established during process qualification until enough data exist for significant variability estimates. It recommends that a statistician or person with adequate statistical training develop the data collection plan and analysis methods, that intra-batch and inter-batch variation be evaluated, and that variation be detected through timely assessment of defect complaints, OOS findings, process deviation reports, process yield variations, batch records, incoming raw material records and adverse event reports.
requirements.system_implications: The eBMR must capture CPPs and CQAs as structured, typed, time-stamped data with units and limits, not free text or scanned PDFs, so they can be trended: intra-batch (time series within a run, e.g., compression force, fill weights) and inter-batch (across batches and sites). The MBR supports a PPQ mode (enhanced sampling plans, protocol reference) and a routine mode with CPV sampling levels. CPV data exports and SPC charts (control limits, Nelson/Western Electric rules) are available with provenance. Material attributes from incoming lots are linked for multivariate analysis.
requirements.verification_test: A PPQ batch executes the enhanced sampling plan and data link to the protocol. A CPV dashboard shows correct control charts, recomputed independently for a sample dataset.

requirements.source: FD&C Act sec. 581(14), 582(a)(9), 582(b)(2) (DSCSA); FDA Guidance 'Product Identifiers Under the DSCSA: Questions and Answers' (final, June 2021)
requirements.clause: Product identifier definition; data carriers; manufacturer obligation to affix to each package and homogeneous case
requirements.requirement: The product identifier is a standardized graphic containing the standardized numerical identifier (NDC plus a unique alphanumeric serial number of up to 20 characters), lot number and expiration date, in both human-readable and machine-readable form. On packages it must be a 2-dimensional data matrix barcode; on homogeneous cases, a linear or 2D data matrix barcode (case carrier rule from the statute's text). Since Nov 27, 2017, manufacturers must affix or imprint a product identifier on each package and homogeneous case of product intended to be introduced in a transaction into commerce. The guidance allows human-readable elements to appear in different locations on the label if space requires.
requirements.system_implications: Applies to Rx finished dosage forms (tablets and injectables); OTC is generally outside DSCSA 'product'. The packaging BPR records the serialization order: the NDC/GTIN, the lot and expiry (from the BPR, not typed in), serial number range or list requested/allocated, commissioned, packed, rejected/decommissioned, sampled, and destroyed. Each printed/verified code is graded (ISO/IEC 15415 for 2D) by the line's vision system, and results are stored. Serial reconciliation equation per lot: commissioned = packed into saleable units + decommissioned (rejects, destroyed, samples, damaged), within zero tolerance for unexplained serials. Aggregation (unit -> bundle -> case -> pallet) parent-child records are stored if the company aggregates (US-DSCSA-03). The lot and expiry in the 2D code must equal the BPR values, with an automated consistency check before release.
requirements.verification_test: Print an intentionally wrong expiry on a test unit -> the vision system rejects it and the line stops. The serial reconciliation report for the test lot balances with zero unexplained serials. Release is blocked if reconciliation fails or commissioning events are missing.

requirements.clause: Transaction information/statement; verification of suspect/illegitimate product; response to verification requests; record retention
requirements.requirement: Manufacturers provide transaction information and statements to subsequent owners and keep them for at least 6 years. They must verify product at package level (including the standardized numerical identifier) when they determine product is suspect or when FDA requests it. They must respond to verification requests from authorized trading partners within 24 hours (secondary-source confirmation). Illegitimate product must be quarantined, investigated and notified (Form 3911 to FDA and trading partners within 24 hours per statute), and investigation records are kept at least 6 years. The 24-hour notification and 6-year retention for investigations are partly from statutory text knowledge.
requirements.system_implications: The packaging record and serialization repository must support a serial -> lot -> BPR lookup in seconds, to answer verification router requests (e.g., VRS) and to check whether a serial was commissioned, decommissioned or shipped. The retention engine must apply the 6-year DSCSA minimum in addition to 211.180 periods (retention = the longer of the two). Suspect-product investigations link to the lot's batch record and genealogy.
requirements.verification_test: Query a random commissioned serial -> the correct lot, expiry and status are returned within the SLA. A decommissioned serial returns 'not verified/decommissioned'. The retention calculation uses max(211.180, 6 years).

requirements.source: FD&C Act sec. 582(g)(1) enhanced drug distribution security; FDA Guidances 'Enhanced Drug Distribution Security at the Package Level Under the DSCSA' (final, Aug 2023) and 'DSCSA Standards for the Interoperable Exchange of Information for Tracing' (final, Sept 2023); FDA exemptions
requirements.clause: Package-level interoperable electronic tracing; EPCIS; exemptions timeline
requirements.requirement: Since Nov 27, 2023 (with a one-year stabilization period to Nov 27, 2024), transaction information must include the product identifier at package level and be exchanged securely, interoperably and electronically. FDA recommends the GS1 EPCIS standard. FDA's exemption for eligible manufacturers and repackagers ended May 27, 2025 (wholesale distributors Aug 27, 2025; dispensers with 26+ FTE Nov 27, 2025; small dispensers exempt to Nov 27, 2026). Manufacturers are therefore fully subject to the enhanced requirements as of Sept 2026. The package-level guidance discusses use of aggregation/inference by trading partners; statute does not explicitly mandate aggregation (interpretation; verify with regulatory counsel).
requirements.system_implications: The packaging eBMR (or the linked L3 line serialization system) must produce EPCIS-compatible commissioning, aggregation, decommissioning and shipping events tied to the batch. The parent-child aggregation hierarchy must be accurate: a vision-verified aggregation step, rework/unpack/repack events recorded, and aggregation errors treated as deviations. Batch release should include a serialization/aggregation completeness check so no unreconciled or unaggregated saleable units exist. The genealogy model must represent the aggregation hierarchy as containment edges (see US-GEN-01).
requirements.verification_test: Build a pallet, unpack a case, and repack -> the EPCIS event history is correct and the final hierarchy is consistent. Release is blocked if any saleable unit is not aggregated when the product is configured for aggregation.

requirements.clause: 201.18 - Drugs; significance of control numbers
requirements.requirement: The lot number on a drug's label should be capable of yielding the complete manufacturing history of the package. An incorrect lot number may be regarded as causing the article to be misbranded.
requirements.system_implications: The printed lot number is sourced only from the BPR lot master: no manual keying on label printers, and the printer receives lot data from the eBMR/L3 over a validated interface. Printed-lot verification is done by vision. Lot numbers resolve to full genealogy (US-210-01). Packaging lots split across multiple packaging orders or sites need explicit sub-lot or packaging-lot linkage so each package lot still yields the complete history.
requirements.verification_test: Try to override the lot number at the printer HMI -> not possible, or detected by the vision check against the BPR. A package lot lookup returns full history, including bulk and intermediate lots.

requirements.source: 21 CFR 201.25 (bar code label requirements) as revised by FDA final rule 'Revising the National Drug Code Format and Drug Label Barcode Requirements' (published March 5, 2026)
requirements.clause: 201.25(c) barcode content and symbology; NDC format (12-digit, 6-4-2) and transition
requirements.requirement: Drug products subject to the bar code rule must carry a barcode containing at least the NDC. Before the 2026 rule, only a linear barcode meeting EAN/UCC or HIBCC standards (or another approved standard) was allowed. The March 5, 2026 final rule standardizes all FDA-assigned NDCs to 12 digits (6-digit labeler, 4-digit product, 2-digit package), effective March 7, 2033. It adds a further transition to March 6, 2036 for labeling updates and depletion of old labels, after which drugs with 10-digit NDCs introduced into commerce may face action. It revises 201.25 to allow linear or nonlinear (e.g., 2D Data Matrix) barcodes that meet recognized standards.
requirements.system_implications: Product and packaging master data must support both 10-digit (current) and 12-digit NDC formats, the NDC-to-GTIN mapping for each, effective-dated NDC changes per SKU, and label artwork versions tied to NDC format. Label and serialization templates must support linear and 2D carriers and verify the encoded NDC equals the master data. Keep historical lots correct: a lot's recorded NDC must never be rewritten when the master NDC changes (effective-dated, immutable per batch).
requirements.verification_test: Change a SKU to a 12-digit NDC effective on a future date -> batches before it keep the old NDC and later batches pick up the new NDC, GTIN and artwork version. Vision verification decodes the NDC from the 2D code and matches master data.

requirements.source: 21 CFR Part 4 (CGMP for combination products), as amended to align with the QMSR (amendments effective Feb 2, 2026 per the medical gases rule summary)
requirements.clause: 4.4(b) streamlined approach for drug-led combination products (e.g., prefilled syringes, autoinjectors)
requirements.requirement: Drug-device combination products manufactured under Part 211 must also meet specified device QS/QMSR provisions (historically 820.20 management responsibility, 820.30 design controls, 820.50 purchasing controls, 820.100 CAPA, 820.170 installation, 820.200 servicing). The exact post-QMSR cross-references were not verified in this pass.
requirements.system_implications: The injectables edition must handle prefilled syringes and autoinjectors: device component genealogy (plunger rod, autoinjector subassembly lots), assembly and labeling steps, device functional IPCs (break-loose/glide force, activation) and design-output linkage. MBR change control must reference design control records where applicable. Confirm the current Part 4 wording after the QMSR alignment.
requirements.verification_test: A combination product MBR requires device component lots and functional test IPCs, and genealogy includes device subassembly lots.

requirements.source: Composite requirement (derived): 21 CFR 210.3 (lot number = complete history), 211.184(c), 211.188(b)(3), 211.130(c), 211.192 (extend investigation to associated batches/products), 211.150/211.196 (distribution for recall), 211.182 (equipment use sequence), 201.18, DSCSA 581/582 (serial -> lot; aggregation)
requirements.clause: Bidirectional genealogy and traceability across materials, equipment, rooms, people, time, packaging hierarchy and distribution
requirements.requirement: The regulations collectively require that, for any lot, the complete manufacturing, control, packing, holding and distribution history can be determined (backward trace), and that from any component lot, equipment, discrepancy or failure all associated batches, other products and consignees can be identified (forward trace and impact analysis for investigations and recalls). DSCSA adds package-level serial identity and parent-child aggregation that must map back to the lot and batch record.
requirements.system_implications: This answers the user's question on graph-based data structures and databases; the recommendation below is engineering judgment, not regulatory text. Genealogy is inherently a directed, time-stamped multigraph. Nodes: material lots, sublots/containers, batches/steps, equipment units, rooms, persons, sterilizer loads, EM samples, serial numbers, cases, pallets, shipments, consignees, deviations. Edges: consumed-by, produced, split/merge, used-equipment, performed-by, sterilized-in, aggregated-into, shipped-in, relates-to-investigation. Queries are variable-depth (multi-stage API -> granulate -> tablets -> coated -> packaged; rework; blending of several intermediate lots; inter-site transfers), so graph modelling fits naturally. The same regulations also require ACID transactional hard stops (211.84, 211.101), an immutable append-only audit trail (11.10(e)), signatures cryptographically bound to record content (11.70), backup and restore as true copies (211.68(b)), retention of 10+ years with readable exports (11.10(b),(c); 211.180), and full validation (211.68, 11.10(a)). Recommended pattern: (1) The system of record is an ACID store (relational, e.g., PostgreSQL, or equivalent) with an append-only, hash-chained event/transaction ledger. Genealogy edges are written in the same transaction as the business event (e.g., a consumption record), so the graph can never disagree with the batch record and there is no dual-write inconsistency. (2) Most genealogy queries run fine as recursive queries (SQL recursive CTEs, or SQL/PGQ property-graph queries where the RDBMS supports them) on indexed edge tables. DSCSA aggregation is shallow (unit -> bundle -> case -> pallet) but high-volume (millions of serials per batch), which relational parent-pointer tables handle well. (3) If scale or latency across many sites needs a dedicated graph database for investigation or recall analytics, make it a derived, read-only, rebuildable projection (CQRS) fed from the ledger via outbox/CDC. Add automated reconciliation (edge counts and hashes per lot) and treat it as GMP-relevant, validated software if its outputs drive GMP decisions such as investigation scope or recall lists. Never make it the sole store of signed records unless it provides equivalent Part 11 audit trail, immutability, point-in-time recovery and long-term export, which most graph databases do not offer natively. (4) Keep genealogy bitemporal (valid time and recording time), so the graph 'as known at release' can be reconstructed after later corrections. (5) Use globally unique IDs with site-scoped business lot numbers to support multi-site graphs, and partition operational data by site with a global genealogy index. 211.180(c) permits central electronic retrieval. (6) The MBR/recipe structure (ISA-88 procedure -> unit procedure -> operation -> phase, with parallel branches) is a DAG that can live as versioned structured documents inside the relational store; it does not require a graph database.
requirements.verification_test: (a) Backward and forward trace for seeded complex scenarios (split, merge, rework, inter-site transfer, repack) returns the exact expected node sets. (b) Reconciliation job: the graph projection (if used) equals ledger-derived edges for 100% of lots, and any drift raises an alert. (c) Impact query performance: forward trace from a high-usage excipient lot across 3 years and N sites completes within the SLA. (d) Point-in-time query reproduces the genealogy as of the release timestamp after a later correction. (e) Rebuild the projection from the ledger in a test environment and compare hashes.

requirements.clause: Record integrity architecture: immutability, contemporaneous commit, timestamps, signature binding
requirements.requirement: Records must be attributable and contemporaneous, changes must not obscure prior values, audit trails must be computer-generated, time-stamped and retained as long as the record, signatures must be inseparably linked to the records they sign, and backups must be exact and secure from alteration or loss.
requirements.system_implications: Engineering judgment derived from the cited rules. Use an event-sourced or append-only versioned record store for GMP data: each entry is an immutable event carrying user, device, UTC server timestamp, site time zone, reason for any change, and a content hash chained to the previous event. The 'current' batch record view is a projection of these events. Signatures reference the hash of the exact record version. A trusted time source (NTP stratum with drift monitoring) must be used, and time-sync failures are alarms. Clock drift on edge devices beyond a threshold blocks data capture. Store UTC and render site-local time with offset (important for multi-site and daylight-saving changes). Database administrators must not be able to alter GMP tables without detection (separation of DBA duties, database activity monitoring, hash verification).
requirements.verification_test: Daylight-saving transition test: events around the change keep a correct order and correct displayed local times. Simulated NTP failure raises an alarm and stops capture on edge devices past the drift threshold. DBA-level update is detected by hash verification and database activity monitoring.

open_questions: Tool limitation: WebFetch was blocked for every domain (ecfr.gov, fda.gov, federalregister.gov, govinfo.gov, law.cornell.edu). All verification relied on WebSearch result extracts of those primary sources. Before design sign-off, a human should open eCFR Part 211 and Part 11, the DI Q&A PDF (fda.gov/media/119570) and the aseptic guidance PDF (fda.gov/media/71026), and confirm clause wording, especially items marked verified=false (US-ASP-03, US-ASP-04, US-ASP-05, US-LYO-01, US-CP-01).

User question (graph databases): the regulations require bidirectional, variable-depth genealogy, which fits a graph model. They also require ACID hard stops, immutable audit trails, signatures bound to records, long-term retention and validation, which fit an ACID ledger. Recommended: a relational/ACID system of record with genealogy edge tables written in the same transaction, plus an optional validated, rebuildable graph projection for analytics (see US-GEN-01). Decisions needed: (a) is a dedicated graph DB justified by expected scale (number of sites, lots per year, serials per batch, recall-query latency target)? (b) if yes, will its outputs drive GMP decisions (investigation scope, recall lists)? If so, it must be validated and continuously reconciled against the system of record.

Is the eBMR delivered as multi-tenant SaaS or single-tenant/customer-hosted? This determines the closed vs open system classification under 11.3/11.30, who controls privileged access, and how the vendor's administrators are kept out of GMP data (DI Q&A admin independence).

211.186(a) requires MPCRs 'for each drug product, including each batch size thereof'. Will the design allow scalable recipes (one MBR covering an approved range of batch sizes), or require a separately approved MBR per batch size? FDA text supports per-size approval. A scalable range needs explicit QA approval of each size or range and justification.

Audit trail review: which data elements are 'critical data' whose changes must be reviewed before final approval (DI Q&A)? This must be defined per MBR template. Also decide whether a review-by-exception UI will be validated as the primary review tool, with full record access always available.

Automated verification under 211.68(c): which operations will be validated as 'automated' so a single verifier suffices (barcode + scale dispensing, automated yield, CIP/SIP, vision-verified labeling)? What is the escalation behavior when automation fails?

Two-person verification: should the verifier be required to be physically present (same room and terminal) and sign within a time window? FDA regulations do not specify this. Also decide whether remote or video-based verification will be allowed; no FDA statement endorsing it was found.

E-signature 'continuous period of controlled system access' (11.200(a)(1)(i)): define the session timeout and whether to require full re-authentication for every signature on shared shop-floor terminals (recommended for verification and release signatures).
